title: James Turrell Was Paid for This Work With a Private Island. He Abandoned Both.
standfirst: Veith Turske asked James Turrell to cut five sky-facing structures into a West Cork hillside and paid him with a 33-acre island in Roaringwater Bay. Turske's business collapsed within the year, Turrell walked off both the job and the island, and what survives today can't even settle on its own name or date.

sections.heading: One Crater, Two Dates, Three Names
sections.body:
The record behind tonight's picture dates it 1991 and calls it Open Sky Garden. Wikipedia's own [catalogue of the artist's work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_James_Turrell_artworks) lists a single Sky Garden from 1992, at the same address outside Skibbereen, County Cork. Most of what has been written about it since — a long-running local newspaper series, a real-estate listing, a scattering of blogs — calls it the Irish Sky Garden instead. All three describe the same crater cut into the same hillside above Roaringwater Bay, and nothing read for this piece explains where the earliest date came from.

The estate's owner, Veith Turske, a German-born, Swiss-based art dealer, bought the land in 1989. Every detailed account of the commission itself — the ten-acre plan, the tunnels, the money — places the actual work in 1992. Whatever existed a year earlier, on paper, under a different name, left no trace in anything read for this piece.

sections.heading: A Ten-Acre, Five-Structure, $4.5 Million Plan
sections.body:
Turske's ambition for Liss Ard went well beyond one crater. He commissioned Turrell to build five separate structures across a ten-acre stretch of the estate, linked by tunnels modelled on the souterrain passages of the ancient ring fort that gave the property its name — Lios Aird, the high fort, in Irish. The budget ran to roughly $4.5 million, to be raised through the charitable Liss Ard Foundation together with a grant from the Irish government.

Turrell had a personal reason to take an interest in Ireland beyond the fee. His [wife, Julia, had ancestry](https://www.irishexaminer.com/lifestyle/artsandculture/arid-40333706.html) in Castletownbere, on the far side of County Cork, and the couple's two youngest children were baptised there. He had also held a [pilot's licence since he was sixteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Turrell) — a man who thought naturally in terms of land seen from above, building something whose whole point was to turn a visitor's eye back up instead.

sections.heading: The Zurich Collapse Turrell Wanted No Part Of
sections.body:
Within months of construction starting, Turske's Zurich art business collapsed into liquidation, leaving creditors unpaid. A Swiss weekly, Zuri Woche, summed up the affair in five words that the [Irish Examiner's own account](https://www.irishexaminer.com/lifestyle/artsandculture/arid-40333706.html) of the project still quotes: "an art scandal of universal proportion." Turrell disassociated himself from Turske and from Liss Ard.

Nothing read for this piece pins down how much of the $4.5 million had actually been spent, or on what, by the time the money stopped arriving. What is documented is the outcome: a plan for five structures across ten acres, reduced permanently to whatever had already gone into the ground before the collapse.

sections.heading: Paid in a Private Island, Then Emptied of It by Night
sections.body:
Turrell's own fee was never cash. "In a deal that recalled the [barter system of ancient Ireland](https://www.irishexaminer.com/lifestyle/artsandculture/arid-40333706.html)," as the Irish Examiner's account puts it, he agreed to build the Sky Garden in exchange for outright ownership of [West Skeam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Skeam_Island), a 33-acre island in Roaringwater Bay. He built a landing strip on its grassy core so he could fly himself in and out.

The base never took. One winter's night, friends from Baltimore, the West Cork village across the water, went out and emptied the island of his belongings, their boats reportedly "down to their gunwales under the weight of antique armoires and telescopes and Turrell's other beloved objects." Edward de Bono, the theorist of lateral thinking, was advertising the island for sale by 2002; the telecoms entrepreneur Leonard Donnelly sold it on again in 2013. Whatever Turrell decided about West Skeam, other people have been deciding about it ever since.

Set that against the other unfinished landscape Turrell is known for. [Roden Crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roden_Crater), the extinct Arizona volcano he has spent decades reshaping into a naked-eye observatory, remains incomplete and is still his. West Skeam, the one piece of land he actually owned outright, he let go of within years.

sections.heading: One Crater Survived, Finished by Strangers, Filed Under a Label He Rejects
sections.body:
Only one of the five planned structures was ever built: a 25-metre oval crater, reached through a tunnel, with a stone plinth at its centre where a visitor can lie down and watch the sky close over the rim. It survives not because of the money that was meant to fund it but despite the lack of it — what stands today, the Irish Examiner reports, "was largely completed under the auspices of a local community employment scheme," not Turrell's own studio. Turrell described the intent, if not the execution, in a line [Roaringwater Journal](https://roaringwaterjournal.com/2014/11/09/sky-garden/) has kept in circulation: "the most important thing is that inside turns into outside and the other way around," in the way the Irish landscape and the Irish sky change places.

The estate around it is now a five-star hotel, bought by American investors for a reported €3.5 million in December 2020 and [listed for sale again](https://thespaces.com/irish-country-hotel-sky-garden-james-turrell-lists-e7-5m/) years later at €7.5 million. None of that history troubles the label the corpus attaches to tonight's picture: Minimalism. It is not a label Turrell has ever claimed for himself — he belongs to the Light and Space movement that grew up around him, Robert Irwin and Mary Corse in 1960s Los Angeles — and it sits oddly on the one Turrell work that is unmistakably, physically, an earthwork. He has said as much about the earthworks label itself, the one Robert Smithson and Michael Heizer wore comfortably and he never did: "I apprehend light — I make events that shape or contain light." Whatever survives outside Skibbereen, cut from the ground and finished by other hands, is filed here as something closer to a canvas.
